t: Paths in Maze That Lead to Same Room: Counting Triangles via Common Neighbors
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We get an undirected graph (rooms 1..n, distinct corridors) and must count unordered triples of rooms that are pairwise connected, i.e. cycles of length 3. Rotations of the same triple count once: Example 1 contains exactly two such cycles, `{4, 1, 3}` and `{1, 2, 4}`, so the answer is 2; Example 2 has no triangle and outputs 0. With `n <= 1000` rooms and up to `5 * 10^4` corridors, blindly testing all `C(1000, 3) ~ 1.7 * 10^8` room triples is wasteful, and the sparse structure suggests intersecting neighbor sets instead.
k: A cycle of length 3 is exactly a triangle: three rooms pairwise adjacent.
Summing |adj[a] ∩ adj[b]| over every corridor (a, b) counts each triangle three times, once per edge, so divide the total by 3.
Intersecting neighbor sets is cheap when you iterate the smaller set and probe the larger.

a.i: Translate the definition literally: enumerate triples i < j < k and count those whose three pairwise edges all exist, using hash sets for O(1) adjacency tests. Skipping early when (i, j) is not an edge prunes most iterations, but the worst case stays cubic.
s: Build hash sets adj[room] of neighbors.
For each i < j < k, first require j to be a neighbor of i, else skip.
Count the triple iff k is a neighbor of both i and j.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case — triple enumeration dominates even with early skipping

a.n: Approach 2: Count Common Neighbors per Corridor (Optimal)
a.i: Triangles through corridor (a, b) correspond one-to-one with common neighbors w of a and b, so the count per corridor is |adj[a] ∩ adj[b]|. Summing over all corridors counts every triangle once per its three edges; dividing by 3 yields the answer. Iterating the smaller adjacency list caps the cost at min(deg a, deg b) lookups.
s: Build adjacency sets from the corridor list.
For each corridor (a, b), iterate the smaller of adj[a], adj[b].
Increment the counter for each element present in the other set.
a.t: O(E * d) — d is the max degree; each corridor costs at most min(deg a, deg b) set probes, very fast for sparse graphs

w:
**Wrap-up**

Go straight to the common-neighbor method; mention the brute force only to show you understand the definition. Pitfalls: forgetting to divide by 3, mishandling 1-indexed rooms, and assuming sorted adjacency (use hash sets, or sort lists and two-pointer intersect). A bitset/boolean-matrix variant trades memory for cache-friendly intersection if needed. Follow-up: counting cycles of length 4 requires a different technique, such as counting pairs of length-2 paths per node.
